outcome: No event since 26 January 2024 settles the characterisation of sums of three integer cubes. As of September–October 2026, Wikipedia (last edited 12 Sep 2026) and Epoch AI (open as of July 2026) still list 114, 390, 627, 633, 732, 921 and 975 as the unresolved cases up to 1000, and no representation of 114 is known. In-window items are a function-field analogue, a heuristic, a conditional almost-all result published in a 2026 journal, two method preprints, an AI challenge listing and an unsigned negative search log; none resolves any case. Earlier cases settled before the window: 74 (2016), 33 (2019), 42 and a third representation of 3 (2019), with 795, 906, 165 and 579 credited to Booker and Sutherland or Booker in 2019 per Wikipedia.
problem_asks: Read as written: (1) determine the set S of integers n for which n = x^3 + y^3 + z^3 has a solution in integers x, y, z, that is, a characterisation of S, not a list. The statement is loose on three points, which the bullet does not settle: whether the cubes must be of integers (the literature reads them so), whether they may be negative or zero, and whether the question is about rational or non-negative cubes, which are different questions. Read in the literature's sense it has these parts: (a) necessity: no n congruent to 4 or 5 mod 9 is representable (elementary; cubes mod 9 are 0, 1, -1; this part is established); (b) sufficiency: every n not congruent to 4 or 5 mod 9 is representable (open for all n; the sources say it is unknown whether the congruence condition is also sufficient). Not asked by the bullet but attached to it in the literature: (c) Heath-Brown's 1992 conjecture that each admissible n has infinitely many representations; (d) the variant with non-negative cubes, whose natural density is unknown per Wikipedia; (e) the rational-cube variant, where every integer is a sum of three rational cubes (classical, per Wikipedia and Epoch).

events.what_happened: Trevor D. Wooley, 'Sums of three cubes, II', arXiv:1502.01944 (v1 6 Feb 2015). Improves moment estimates for cubic Weyl sums for 4 <= s <= 8 and, as a consequence, gives an improved lower bound on the number of integers up to X that are sums of three natural-number (non-negative) cubes. Discovered during the search of the Wikipedia article's variant list; not a representation of any specific n.
events.revisions: v1 only (6 Feb 2015).
events.delivers: A lower bound on the count of integers up to X expressible as a sum of three non-negative cubes. This is the non-negative-cube variant, not the all-integer question. It establishes no specific representation and no case of the bullet.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks: no characterisation, no representation of any n, and the density question for non-negative cubes is not settled by this bound.
events.direction: Neutral on the bullet. It concerns a neighbouring variant (non-negative cubes) and moves a count of that variant's representable integers, not the bullet's set.

events.what_happened: Sander G. Huisman, 'Newer sums of three cubes', arXiv:1604.07746 (v1 26 Apr 2016, only version). Extends the search for x^3+y^3+z^3 = k to all k < 1000 with |x|,|y|,|z| up to 10^15; reports the first solution for k = 74 and 966 new solutions; states that only k = 33 and k = 42 remain open for k < 100. Wikipedia credits Huisman with solving 74.
events.revisions: v1 only (26 Apr 2016).
events.delivers: A representation of 74: closes the case k = 74 (one of the open k < 1000 values in the 2009 list). Restricted to the search box (|x|,|y|,|z| up to 10^15) and to k < 1000 for the other values; no claim for k >= 1000 and no general characterisation.
events.remains: All other n, including all n >= 1000 and every admissible n not yet searched; the characterisation and infinitude parts. The open cases from 2009 remaining after this paper (per Wikipedia and Huisman's abstract) include 33 and 42 as small cases, which were settled in 2019.

events.what_happened: Victor Y. Wang, 'Sums of cubes and the Ratios Conjectures', arXiv:2108.03398 (v1 7 Aug 2021; v2 19 Apr 2023, which changed the title and 'moved some material elsewhere'; the arXiv page shows no journal reference). Studies N, the number of integral solutions of x1^3+...+x6^3 = 0 in expanding regions. The abstract (opened, in parts) says the softest hypotheses (Ratios and Square-free Sieve Conjectures and standard L-function hypotheses) 'imply conjectures of Hooley and Manin on N, and show that almost all integers a not congruent to +/-4 mod 9 are sums of three cubes.' Published as 'Zeta statistics at the square-root barrier for cubes', Journal of the Association for Mathematical Research 4(1) (2026) 183-236, DOI 10.56994/JAMR.004.001.004; the JAMR page gives the printed date as 03/12/2026 and its abstract says 'We give applications to sums of three cubes'. I did not confirm that the JAMR article is the same work as the arXiv preprint, although the claims match in substance.
events.revisions: v1 7 Aug 2021; v2 19 Apr 2023 (title changed; current). Published as JAMR 4(1) (2026) under a different title.
events.delivers: Conditional on the Ratios and Square-free Sieve Conjectures (and, for the epsilon-version, automorphy and GRH for Hasse-Weil L-functions): a density-one statement that almost all integers a not congruent to +/-4 mod 9 are sums of three cubes. It settles no specific n, is conditional, and leaves the exceptional density-zero set open. It is not unconditional and does not characterise the set.
events.remains: Every specific admissible n (including 114, 390, 627, 633, 732, 921, 975), the exceptional density-zero set, the unconditional result, the characterisation, and the infinitude part.

events.what_happened: Epoch AI's FrontierMath: Open Problems page lists a 'Sum of Three Cubes' challenge (opened). It asks for (a) a new representation of 3, beyond (1,1,1), (4,4,-5) and the Booker-Sutherland triple, and (b) integers whose cubes sum to 114; it says the smallest n whose representability is unknown is 114, with status 'open as of July 2026' and that no solution is presently known; it says 'it is possible that a clever idea is needed for AI to solve this problem'. Submissions are checked by exact arithmetic. The page lists the tags Unsolved, Diophantine, Integer Solution, Record Breaking. Epoch's Open Problems pilot launched 27 Jan 2026 with 14 problems (Epoch substack, opened); the cube problem is not named in that post, and its addition date is not established.

events.what_happened: Undated research log 'A practical search strategy for three cubes summing to 114' on kuber.studio (Math Gambling project; links to the Kuberwastaken/math-gambling repository; opened). Describes a 'phase3' local search for x^3+y^3+z^3 = 114 with 12 local workers and about 39.4 million curve-interval checks per second; reports that no representation of 114 has been found; reports a stronger square sieve rejected (no measured speedup); reports one held-out representation of 69 in a test experiment (not presented as new); and proposes a geometric approach not yet implemented. The date (about 9 Sep 2026) is inferred from an archive path and a deadline on the page, not stated.

events.doubts: Unsigned research log with no named author; compute and throughput figures are self-reported; a search that finds nothing is not evidence about whether 114 is representable.

disputes.summary: Booker's 33 result: a search summary says Tim Browning posted the solution on his homepage around March 2019 and some readers took him to be the discoverer; the arXiv v1 of Booker's paper is dated 11 Mar 2019. Not verified against the source of that claim, which I did not open.

The open-case lists differ. A 2019 ScienceAlert article lists 114, 165, 390, 579, 627, 633, 732, 906, 921 and 975 (and in another write-up 795), while Wikipedia (edited 12 Sep 2026) says the only unresolved cases up to 1000 are 114, 390, 627, 633, 732, 921 and 975, and credits 165, 579, 795 and 906 to 2019 work. The 2009 Elsenhans-Jahnel list (per Wikipedia) was 33, 42, 74, 114, 165, 390, 579, 627, 633, 732, 795, 906, 921 and 975.

The first representation of 3 is dated variously: Epoch's page says the Booker-Sutherland triple is from 2019; Wikipedia says 2019; PNAS was published in 2021 (MIT News, 11 Mar 2021); the arXiv version is dated 2 Jul 2020. I date the first public write-up by the Simons Collaboration post (September 2019, month inferred from the post's URL and MIT's 'two weeks later' account), not by the 2020 arXiv or 2021 PNAS.

The triples in the sources have formatting artifacts. The 42 triple is printed with an extra digit in some outlets; the 3 triple's first coordinate is printed as 5699368212219623807203 (22 digits), where the cube sign appears to have become a digit. The triples have not been arithmetically checked by me; the shell check was denied.

Wang's arXiv preprint (2108.03398, 2021, retitled 2023) is 'Sums of cubes and the Ratios Conjectures'; the 2026 JAMR article with matching claims is 'Zeta statistics at the square-root barrier for cubes'. I did not confirm they are the same paper.

summary: Sources read: Wikipedia's 'Sums of three cubes' article (edited 12 Sep 2026), Epoch AI's FrontierMath page for the problem (status 'open as of July 2026'), the primary arXiv abstracts for the preprints listed above, the Bristol press release (6 Sep 2019), the Simons Collaboration post on 3, MIT News (11 Mar 2021), the JAMR article page, the Selecta/ISTA record, the Math Gambling 114 search log, and two Epoch-related news pieces. Several primary PDFs (the PNAS paper, Miller-Woollett 1955, Huisman's ancillary data, Booker's 33 identity, Flores et al., Bagis, and Epoch's own PDF) returned no readable text to me, and the PNAS page returned HTTP 403, so their content is taken only from abstracts or secondary reports and is marked as such. Judgement calls: (1) The bullet's scope is read as the all-integer question. Its variants (non-negative cubes, rational cubes) and the infinitude conjecture are recorded as separate events or context. (2) Single-case solutions (74, 33, 42, 3, 795, 906, 165, 579) are recorded as events that close individual cases; none moves the characterisation. (3) Wang's conditional 'almost all' result (2021, JAMR 2026) is the closest thing in the record to a result about the bullet itself. It is conditional and settles no individual case, so I record it as a density statement, not a resolution; whether its 2026 publication is an in-window event depends on the date rule, and I have dated it to the arXiv v1 (2021) per the rule, with the JAMR publication in checked_by. (4) Browning-Wilsch (2024) and the two Browning-Glas-Wang function-field papers (2024) are heuristic or analogue work and are recorded as discounted events. (5) Wadhawan (arXiv Dec 2025) is a method preprint whose arXiv record gives a 2020 journal reference; if that 2020 article exists and carries this method, the event moves before the window. I could not verify it. (6) Flores et al. (2021) claims in the abstract a procedure to decide existence for a given n. Whether it works is not checkable from the abstract, and it is the single item in the record whose claim, if true for all n, would bear directly on the bullet; no outside engagement was found. (7) The Epoch challenge and the kuber.studio log are not results and are recorded as non-events for the purpose of the record. AI involvement: I found no AI system credited with any result on this problem, including any sum-of-three-cubes result in the window. The AI-related items nearby are: Epoch's AI-targeted challenge (no system credited); a Sept 2026 progressiverobot.com tag-page teaser about an unconfirmed leaked Gemini 'Mathematica' build that it says identifies 'the open number-theory problem in the leaked trace' but does not name the problem; I could not tie the leak to this problem, and the source is a teaser, not a primary account. Other AI items that do not concern this problem: Stevanovic and Stevanovic (MATCH 2026, ChatGPT on a graph-theory problem with a Diophantine condition); Grechuk's list of open Diophantine equations (arXiv 2404.08518 landing page, with ChatGPT 5.4 credited for solutions to other cubic equations, not sums of three cubes, which I could not read in full); and Epoch's first AI solution on FrontierMath: Open Problems (a Ramsey-type problem). Close calls on 'none found': the kuber.studio log uses a 'learned scheduler' (machine learning inside the author's own search code) and the Lazov-Vetsov paper uses particle-swarm and simulated-annealing optimisers (ACM class I.2.8). I recorded both as no named AI system, but a judging pass might read them as AI involvement in searches that found nothing. Dates for the Booker 2019 events are from the arXiv v1 date (11 Mar 2019) and the Bristol press release (6 Sep 2019); the 2019 795/906/165/579 entries are year-only because I could not find their first written argument.
competing_reading: (a) Wang's conditional almost-all result (arXiv 2021, JAMR 2026) could be read as a substantive advance on the bullet, since it is a density-one statement about sums of three cubes and was published in 2026. The reading against it: it is conditional on Ratios and Square-free Sieve Conjectures, settles no individual n, and its arXiv date is 2021, before the window. (b) The Booker-Sutherland 2019-2021 work could be read as moving a quantity the bullet asks about (how many representations, or which small k are settled) and therefore as in-window if its PNAS publication (2021) were the date. The reading against it: PNAS is 2021, not in the window; and it settles only individual cases, which the bullet does not ask for. (c) The Browning-Wilsch heuristic and the Browning-Glas-Wang analogues could be read as progress because they sharpen predictions and the function-field method; the reading against is that heuristics and analogues do not establish any case. (d) Wadhawan's 'seed equation' method could be read as a general parametrisation if its body makes such a claim; the abstract does not, and the 2020 journal reference would move the event before the window. (e) Flores et al.'s decision procedure could be read as a complete solution if correct for all n; the abstract states it as a procedure for a given unknown n, and I could not check the body, so I can not say whether it has such a claim or whether it works. (f) On AI: one could read the Epoch challenge listing and the 2026 leak as AI involvement in this problem. The reading against it is that neither reports any AI result, and the leak does not name this problem.
what_would_settle_it: (1) An exact-arithmetic check of the triples for 33, 42, 3 (third representation) and 74, and a representation of 114 or any other of the seven listed open cases, which would close that case. (2) An unconditional proof for almost all admissible n, or a proof of Heath-Brown's conjecture, which would bear on the characterisation. (3) The full text of the JAMR article (to confirm it is the same as arXiv 2108.03398 and what its hypotheses are) and of the PNAS paper (to confirm which values of k it newly settles and the stated 'completes the search' scope). (4) The body of arXiv 2103.17037 (Flores et al.) to see whether it claims a decision procedure for all n and whether it has been checked by anyone. (5) The body of arXiv 2512.15763 and the Mathematical Forum 28(2) (2020) reference, to fix the date of the seed-equation method. (6) The 2016 ancillary file and the 1955 table, to confirm the historical list of open cases. (7) Wikipedia's January 2024 revision and Epoch's changelog, to fix which of 165, 579, 795, 906 and the 2009 list were open at the frozen revision, and the date the cube problem entered Epoch's Open Problems. (8) A later status check on Wikipedia and Epoch's problem page, since both report 114 as open as of mid-2026.
